nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Feeds can reduce friction between rewards and remove natural stopping points. A person may keep checking for a worthwhile clip even after several uninteresting ones. The design makes continuing the default; stopping requires a fresh decision. That can shift behaviour without making every episode a sign of addiction.

Frequent viewing is not automatically compulsive or harmful. The relevant question is whether the behaviour repeatedly conflicts with the person's goals.
nodes.sources: Alter (2017), Irresistible; research on persuasive design and self-control.

nodes.sources: Alter (2017), Irresistible; research on persuasive design and self-control.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
An endless feed removes natural stopping cues while unpredictable interesting content makes the next item seem worth checking. The environment increases the work required to stop.

Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
